query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An atomistic simulation that explicitly incorporates oxygen-induced defect scattering will predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than traditional analytical models based on perfect crystals across both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Develop and implement a computational model—via enhanced density functional theory (DFT) or parameterized interatomic potentials—that explicitly includes the scattering effects of oxygen defects in the alloy.
generation.conditions: The model is applied to specimens with ~1 wt.% oxygen over two temperature windows: a low-temperature regime (0–200 K) and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K), where experimental conductivity measurements already exist.
generation.structural_mediator: Oxygen impurity sites acting as scattering centers, which modify electron and phonon transport compared to an ideal, defect‐free lattice.
generation.mechanism: Incorporation of oxygen defects into the simulation alters the carrier scattering mechanisms. At low temperatures, enhanced impurity scattering reduces conductivity relative to defect‐free predictions, while at high temperatures, additional phonon scattering and defect–lattice interactions introduce non-ideal conductivity behavior—effects that traditional analytical models fail to capture.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new model will yield conductivity predictions that show a reduction at 0–200 K and a distinct, experimentally consistent trend in the 300–1200 K range, closely matching the measurements on oxygen-containing samples and outperforming predictions based on perfect crystal assumptions.
generation.baseline: Analytical predictions based on perfect, defect‐free bulk HfNbTaTiZr crystals.
generation.boundary: Applicability is expected to hold for specimens with similar oxygen impurity levels (~1 wt.%) within the specified temperature ranges (0–200 K and 300–1200 K). Predictions outside these regimes or for different impurity concentrations remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of conductivity changes is uncertain because of potential variability in the spatial distribution and local environment of oxygen impurities, as well as approximations in the computational treatment of defect scattering.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform high-precision electrical conductivity measurements on bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen over the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges. In parallel, compute the conductivity using the new atomistic model that includes oxygen defect scattering. Compare the simulation outputs to the experimental data for both temperature regimes.
measurements: Electrical conductivity as a function of temperature
Characterization of oxygen impurity distribution via techniques such as TEM or XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental conductivity measurements deviate by more than an estimated tolerance (e.g., >20% discrepancy) from the model’s predictions in either temperature regime, the hypothesis that incorporating oxygen-induced defect scattering improves prediction accuracy will be falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5.
